name: Transient ischaemic attack

matching.reasoningTemplate: Transient focal neurological deficit that fully resolves suggests a TIA — high short-term stroke risk.

redFlags: High early stroke risk — urgent TIA clinic / admission

clinicalPearls: TIA classically produces 'negative' symptoms (transient loss of function); positive sensory symptoms or involuntary movements point instead to seizure (p.3378).
Most TIAs last under 1 hour, well within the historical 24-hour window (p.3448).

About 25% of symptomatic internal carotid disease is heralded by recurrent transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax), typically described as a horizontal shade sweeping down or up across one eye, lasting a few minutes (p.3430).
A high-pitched carotid bruit fading into diastole suggests a tight stenosis; paradoxically the bruit may fade or vanish as occlusion becomes imminent and flow drops (p.3430).
Causes of TIA and ischaemic stroke are identical, so the diagnostic evaluation of a TIA should parallel that of a completed stroke (p.3448).
harrison.pathophysiology: A TIA results from transient focal cerebral ischaemia when blood flow falls for longer than several seconds; neurons lack glycogen so deficits appear within seconds, but because the occluded vessel reopens and flow is restored before infarction occurs, symptoms resolve completely. Mechanisms mirror ischaemic stroke: emboli to the brain (cardiac or proximal arterial source) or in-situ thrombosis of an intracranial vessel. Small-vessel (lacunar) TIAs may recur several times a day and last only minutes (Harrison 22e p.3428, 3448, 3447).
additionalDifferentials: Seizure (esp. ongoing focal seizure without convulsive activity) — positive symptoms and a marching spread over seconds favour seizure (p.3378, p.3428)
Migraine, including acephalgic migraine even in older first-time patients — slower march over minutes with headache, nausea or scintillating visual symptoms (p.3428)
Intracranial tumour presenting acutely via haemorrhage, seizure or hydrocephalus (p.3428)
Metabolic encephalopathy — fluctuating mental status without focal findings (p.3428)
Stroke recrudescence — fever/sepsis unmasking a prior deficit that clears as infection is treated (p.3428)
nonInfectiousMimics: Seizure (focal, may mimic transient deficit) (p.3378, p.3428)
Migraine / acephalgic migraine with transient aura (p.3428)
Syncope from systemic hypotension (cardiac arrhythmia, sepsis, haemorrhagic shock) (p.3428)
additionalInvestigations: CT- or MRI-based angiography of neck and intracranial vessels to assess large-vessel stenosis/occlusion (MRA is highly sensitive for extracranial carotid stenosis but tends to overestimate severity) (p.3445, p.3430)
Echocardiography (transthoracic or transoesophageal), with bubble-contrast/agitated-saline study to detect right-to-left shunt (PFO/ASD) for suspected paradoxical embolism (p.3445)
Cardiac telemetry following the initial ECG; ambulatory/prolonged ECG monitoring to detect intermittent atrial fibrillation if none is found in hospital (p.3445)
Retinal/funduscopic exam for cholesterol (Hollenhorst) plaques and examination of cervical/peripheral vessels and heart (p.3445)
Baseline labs: CBC, ESR, electrolytes, glucose, lipid profile, creatinine/BUN, PT/PTT, urinalysis, chest x-ray (p.3445)
redFlags: Most strokes after a TIA occur within the first 2 days — the early window is the highest-risk period and warrants urgent (not deferred) workup (p.3448)
Stuttering or crescendo course of small-vessel TIAs heralding lacunar infarct can progress to severe permanent disability (p.3447)
Amaurosis fugax indicates a symptomatic internal carotid source needing prompt carotid evaluation (p.3430)
harrison.prognosis: Stroke risk after a TIA is approximately 10-15% within the first 3 months, with most events occurring in the first 2 days; this early risk is well predicted by the ABCD2 score, so urgent evaluation and treatment are justified (Harrison 22e p.3448).
pitfalls: A TIA is a clinical diagnosis: a normal brain imaging study does NOT rule it out (p.3448).

If a relevant infarction is seen on imaging, the event is reclassified as a stroke regardless of how briefly symptoms lasted — the modern definition is tissue-based, not purely time-based (p.3428, p.3448).
Patients with carotid/vertebrobasilar TIA may report symptoms 'in one eye' when the deficit is actually a homonymous hemifield loss affecting both eyes (p.3430-equivalent / cortical visual TIA).
Acephalgic migraine can mimic TIA even with no prior migraine history and even after age 65 (p.3428).
harrison.severityClassification: ABCD2 score (Harrison 22e p.3448) stratifies early stroke risk after TIA: 1 point each for Age >=60, BP (SBP >140 or DBP >90 mmHg), and Diabetes; for Clinical features 2 points for unilateral weakness or 1 for speech disturbance without weakness; for Duration 2 points for >=60 min or 1 for 10-59 min. The 3-month stroke rate rises with the total: ~0% at score 0-1, ~3% at 2-3, ~8% at 4, ~12% at 5, ~17% at 6, and ~22% at 7.
